Achieving Robust Channel Estimation Neural Networks on Doppler effects by Designed Training Data

Dianxin Luan Affiliation: Institute for Imaging, Data and Communications Affiliation: University of Edinburgh    John Thompson Affiliation: Edinburgh, EH9 3JL, United Kingdom Affiliation: d.luan3017@gmail.com, J.S.Thompson@ed.ac.uk
Abstract

Channel estimation is crucial in wireless communication systems. Many existing works train and test their models using the same or similar channel. However, practical channels are infinitely diverse and time-variant while data-driven algorithms often degrade on new and previously unseen channels. This prohibits the practical implementation of neural networks for channel estimation, particularly in high speed scenarios characterized by rapidly channel profile changes and very high Doppler shifts. Online training can fine-tune models to adapt to new channels, but requires high computation resource and incurs significant latency for physical-layer devices. Moreover, online training cannot exhaustively cover all possible channels because there are infinitely many possible channels. Therefore, we investigate the ability of neural networks to generalize to wireless channels. This paper proposes design criteria to generate synthetic training data, which guaranty that the resulting networks perform robustly across wireless channels, especially for very high Doppler shifts and different Doppler spectra. It ensures that offline-trained neural networks require no prior information or online training to precisely estimate the new channels. To demonstrate general applicability, we use neural networks with different levels of complexity to show that the generalization achieved appears to be independent of architecture. From simulation results, neural networks achieve a certain performance across wireless channels with different unseen power delay profiles (PDP) and Doppler shifts.

1 Introduction

For sixth-generation (6G) wireless communications and beyond, orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) is expected to continue as the baseband modulator Wang and others (2023). Therefore, acquiring precise channel state information (CSI) is essential for reliable links that provide high data rates. Channel estimation refers to the process of estimating channel state information of the propagation environments between the transmitter and the receiver end. The CSI estimate is subsequently used to mitigate channel distortions and recover the transmitted data. Least-squares (LS) and minimum mean squared error (MMSE) methods are widely investigated for channel estimation (CE) Van De Beek et al. (1995); Edfors et al. (1998); Li et al. (1998); Srivastava et al. (2004). However, conventional approaches struggle to meet the increasingly stringent data-rate and reliability system requirements, motivating the exploration of machine learning approaches for overall system optimization Ye et al. (2017); Kim et al. (2018b); Kim et al. (2018a); Neumann et al. (2018); Kim et al. (2020); Baur et al. (2024); Allaparapu et al. (2026); Luan and Thompson (2026). Unlike conventional methods that aim for closed-form mathematical expressions, neural network approaches learn nonlinear mappings directly from the data and often achieve locally optimal but improved performance, such as ChannelNet Soltani et al. (2019). With the development of the attention mechanism, Luan and Thompson (2022); Luan and Thompson (2023a) proposed an encoder-decoder architecture, called Channelformer, to utilize the transformer encoder Vaswani et al. (2017) to focus on the critical subset of input LS elements. However, data-driven algorithms often degrade on new channels. This instability prohibits the real-world implementation of neural networks for time-variant channels. To adapt to channel variations while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, Kong et al. (2025) proposed a continuous learning-based channel estimation solution that preserves previously learned knowledge through several subnetworks. A VAE-assisted unsupervised out-of-distribution (OOD) detector identifies unseen channels, after which a new subnetwork is rapidly adapted by using only a few online samples. To fine-tune neural channel estimator under varying channel conditions, Wang et al. (2026) proposed a two-branch masked autoencoder that enables label-free online training through self-supervised reconstruction of randomly masked resource elements. Wang et al. (2025) proposed a federated collaborative learning solution with pruning for neural receivers while mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

1.1 Problem statement

Although online training methods can fine-tune offline-trained neural networks to adapt to new channels, they have several critical drawbacks as follows:

1) Latency and computational consumption: Collecting training samples and parameters updating will result in significant and unavoidable latency. For example, the slot length is between 0.0625 milliseconds and 1 millisecond as defined in the 3GPP TS 38.211 document and the receiver needs at least 62.5-1,000 milliseconds to collect each 1,000 examples. Moreover, the computational cost and latency of the training process are typically high, so it is difficult for battery-powered terminals to update neural networks promptly, especially in highly dynamic environments. Moreover, online training cannot exhaustively cover all wireless channels as the set of possible channels is infinite.

2) Interpolation capability and performance loss: The superior performance achieved by channel estimation neural networks is primarily down to their interpolation capability for OFDM. However, this good performance cannot be retained through online training because training requires the ground-truth channel matrix for the entire data packet, including the ground-truth channel matrix at both the vacant pilot positions (frequency-domain interpolation) and the data symbols (time-domain interpolation). The complete and ground-truth channel matrix of the environment channel is unavailable in practical systems, which indicates the loss of this superior performance. As shown in Fig.7a and Fig.7b of Luan and Thompson (2025) (provided in Appendix A), it effectively addresses the generalization of neural networks to different channel power delay profiles (PDP), i.e. retaining frequency-domain interpolation capability on unseen channels. For time-domain interpolation, it is challenging because statistical models are inaccurate, cumbersome and difficult to handle Nissel et al. (2018), and the basis expansion model Borah and Hart (1999) is used for time-variant channels. Therefore, offline-trained neural networks are also expected to generalize well to different Doppler shifts and Doppler spectra, to retain time-domain interpolation capability on unseen channels.

1.2 Main contribution and notion

The key contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    This paper proposes design criteria to generate synthetic training data which guarantees that trained neural networks generalize well to different Doppler spectra and Doppler shifts. Regardless of the channels which neural networks operate on, offline-trained neural networks achieve stable performance without any knowledge of this channel at the design time. This provides robust generalization to previously unseen channels.

  • •

    Ground-truth and complete channel matrices can be still used as labels because the training channel is synthetically generated. By being trained with the complete channel matrix, neural networks retain precise interpolation capabilities in both frequency and time domain for superior estimate performance when operating on new, previously unseen channels.

2 System configuration and Propagation channels

This paper considers an OFDM cellular system with a subcarrier spacing of fs​p​a​c​ef_{space} kHz. The source signal is processed by a Quadrature Phase Shift Keying (QPSK) modulator. The QPSK symbols are assigned to the data subcarriers. The pilot signals are known to the receiver, and the vacant pilot subcarriers are set to 0. Each slot consists of NfN_{f} subcarriers and NsN_{s} OFDM symbols. By following the 5G NR specifications in 3GPP TS 38.211, a single-symbol demodulation reference signal (DM-RS) pattern with three additional positions is deployed. The 2nd, 5th, 8th and 11th OFDM symbols are reserved for pilots (Np​i​l​o​t=4N_{pilot}=4). For each pilot OFDM symbol, the second subcarriers of each indices of Ls=2L_{s}=2 subcarriers is reserved for pilot subcarriers. The inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) converts the slot signal from the frequency domain to the time domain. Then the Cyclic-Prefix (CP, of length LCPL_{\mathrm{CP}} samples) is added to the front of each symbol to eliminate intersymbol interference (ISI) but it cannot mitigate intercarrier interference (ICI) caused by Doppler shifts. The channel model is a multipath channel with MM paths with impulse response of

h⁡(τ,t)=∑m=0M−1am​ej​2​π​fd,m​t​δ​(τ−τm​Ts),h(\tau,t)=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}a_{m}e^{j2\pi f_{d,m}t}\delta(\tau-\tau_{m}T_{s}), (1)

where am∼𝒞​𝒩​(0,Am)a_{m}\sim\mathcal{CN}(0,A_{m}) is the path gain of the mt​hm^{th} path, AmA_{m} is the average path power, τm\tau_{m} is the corresponding delay normalized by the sampling period TsT_{s}, fd,mf_{d,m} is the Doppler shift and fdf_{d} is the maximum Doppler shift. The time-varying channel coefficient of the mmth path is denoted by

γm​(t)=am​ej​2​π​fd,m​t.\gamma_{m}(t)=a_{m}e^{j2\pi f_{d,m}t}. (2)

Conditioned on the Doppler shift, γm​(t)\gamma_{m}(t) is a complex Gaussian process. Doppler shifts {fd,m}m=0M−1\{f_{d,m}\}_{m=0}^{M-1} are independently sampled from the normalized Doppler spectrum S⁡(f)S(f) for channel realizations (∀m,|fd,m|≤fd\forall m,|f_{d,m}|\leq f_{d}) and are independent of path gains. Conventionally, the Doppler spectrum S⁡(f)S(f) of wireless channels is characterized by the Jakes model, which has the theoretical formula of

S⁡(f)=1π​fd​1−(f/fd)2,|f|<fd,S(f)=\frac{1}{\pi f_{d}\sqrt{1-\left(f/f_{d}\right)^{2}}},\qquad|f|<f_{d}, (3)

and S⁡(f)=0S(f)=0 otherwise. Therefore, the nnth sampled time-domain 𝐡⁡(n,t)\mathbf{h}(n;t) is

𝐡⁡(n,t)=∑m=0M−1am​ej​2​π​fd,m​t​e−j​π​n+(Nf−1)​τmNf​sin⁡(π​τm)sin⁡(πNf​(τm−n)).\mathbf{h}(n;t)=\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}a_{m}e^{j2\pi f_{d,m}t}e^{-j\pi\frac{n+(N_{f}-1)\tau_{m}}{N_{f}}}\frac{\sin(\pi\tau_{m})}{\sin(\frac{\pi}{N_{f}}(\tau_{m}-n))}. (4)

The sampled PDP 𝐩⁡(n)=𝔼⁡(∣𝐡⁡(n)∣2)\mathbf{p}(n)=\mathbb{E}\left(\mid\mathbf{h}(n)\mid^{2}\right), if the channel is invariant within single OFDM symbol duration ToT_{o}, then the sampled signal 𝐲=𝐡⊗𝐱+𝐧\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{h}\otimes\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{n}, where 𝐧\mathbf{n} is additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and 𝐱\mathbf{x} is the transmitted signal. Each slot is assigned a new channel realization. After removing the CP, the receiver converts the time-domain data to the frequency-domain by the FFT operation. Assuming that ∀τm≤LC​P\forall{\tau_{m}}\leq L_{CP}, the channel gain at the kkth subcarrier and llth symbol is

𝐇⁡(k,l)=1Nf​∑m=0M−1am​ej​2​π​fd,m​To​l​e−j​2​π​k​τmNf.\mathbf{H}\left(k,l\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{f}}}\sum_{m=0}^{M-1}a_{m}e^{j2\pi f_{d,m}T_{o}l}e^{-j2\pi\frac{k\tau_{m}}{N_{f}}}. (5)

for k=0,1,…,Nf−1k=0,1,...,N_{f}-1 and ToT_{o} is one complete OFDM symbol period including the CP. Then E{𝐇k,l𝐇k′,l′∗}=rt(l−l′)rf(k−k′)E\{\mathbf{H}_{k,l}\mathbf{H}_{k_{{}^{\prime}},l{{}^{\prime}}}^{*}\}=r_{t}(l-l^{\prime})r_{f}(k-k^{\prime}) where rf,rtr_{f},r_{t} is the frequency and time correlation that are separable as shown in (26). For Jakes model, rt​(Δ​l)=J0​(2​π​fd​To​Δ​l)r_{t}(\Delta l)=J_{0}(2\pi f_{d}T_{o}\Delta l) is the zeroth-order Bessel function. The received frequency domain signal at kkth subcarrier and llth OFDM symbol, 𝐘⁡(k,l)\mathbf{Y}(k,l), is of the form:

𝐘⁡(k,l)=𝐇⁡(k,l)​𝐗​(k,l)+𝐍⁡(k,l),\mathbf{Y}(k,l)=\mathbf{H}(k,l)\mathbf{X}(k,l)+\mathbf{N}(k,l), (6)

where 𝐍∼𝒞​𝒩​(𝟎,σN2​𝐈Nf)\mathbf{N}\sim\mathcal{CN}(\mathbf{0},\ \sigma_{N}^{2}\mathbf{I}_{N_{f}}), 𝐇∈ℂNf×Ns\mathbf{H}\in\mathbb{C}^{{N_{f}}\times N_{s}} is the channel matrix and σX2=E⁡{(Nf​Ns)−1​‖𝐗‖F2}\sigma_{X}^{2}=E\{(N_{f}N_{s})^{-1}\left\Arrowvert\mathbf{X}\right\Arrowvert_{F}^{2}\}. The received pilot signal is then extracted to provide a reference for channel estimate. The recovered signal will be filtered to remove the channel effects.

2.1 Propagation channels

Wireless channels are modeled as multipath Rayleigh fading channels operating at a carrier frequency fsf_{s} of 3.5GHz in the n78 band, which is specified in 3GPP TS 38.104. The extended pedestrian A (EPA), extended vehicular A (EVA) and extended typical urban (ETU) channels are defined in 3GPP 36.101. The other example channel PDPs for simulations are given in Table. 2.

2.2 Channel estimation and methods

Channel estimation is to estimate the channel matrix 𝐇\mathbf{H}. To minimize the distance between the received signal and the channel-distorted signal, LS estimate at the kkth subcarrier is

𝐇^𝐥𝐬​(k)=Yk​Xk−1,\mathbf{\hat{H}_{ls}}(k)=Y_{k}X_{k}^{-1}, (7)

where Yk,XkY_{k},X_{k} denotes the received and transmitted signals for the kkth subcarrier. This paper applies bilinear interpolation on 𝐇^𝐥𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐨𝐭∈ℂNfLs×Np​i​l​o​t\mathbf{\hat{H}_{ls}^{pilot}}\in\mathbb{C}^{\frac{N_{f}}{L_{s}}\times N_{pilot}} (at the pilot positions) to predict the complete channel matrix. To arg⁡min𝐇∥𝐇−𝐇𝐥𝐬∥2F\mathop{\arg\!\min_{\mathbf{H}}}\Arrowvert\mathbf{H}-\mathbf{H_{ls}}\Arrowvert^{2}_{F}, MMSE estimate for OFDM symbols is computed by

𝐇^𝐌𝐌𝐒𝐄=𝐖H​𝐇^𝐥𝐬,W=(𝐑𝐇𝐇+(σN2σX2)​𝐈Nf)−1​𝐑𝐇𝐇,\mathbf{\hat{H}_{MMSE}}=\mathbf{W}^{H}\mathbf{\hat{H}_{ls}},W=\left(\mathbf{R_{HH}}+\left(\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{\sigma_{X}^{2}}\right)\mathbf{I}_{N_{f}}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{R_{HH}}, (8)

where 𝐑𝐇𝐇∈ℂNf×Nf\mathbf{R_{HH}}\in\mathbb{C}^{{N_{f}}\times{N_{f}}} is the channel autocorrelation matrix with 𝐑𝐇𝐇​(k1,k2)=E⁡{𝐇k1​𝐇k2∗}\mathbf{R_{HH}}(k_{1},k_{2})=E\{\mathbf{H}_{k_{1}}\mathbf{H}_{k_{2}}^{*}\} for ∀k1,k2∈[0,Nf−1]\forall{k_{1},k_{2}\in[0,N_{f}-1]}, and E{𝐇k,l𝐇k′,l′∗}=rt(l−l′)rf(k−k′)E\{\mathbf{H}_{k,l}\mathbf{H}_{k_{{}^{\prime}},l{{}^{\prime}}}^{*}\}=r_{t}(l-l^{\prime})r_{f}(k-k^{\prime}) as shown in (5) where rf,rtr_{f},r_{t} is the frequency and time correlation. σN2σX2\frac{\sigma_{N}^{2}}{\sigma_{X}^{2}} is the inverse signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and σ2\sigma^{2} denotes the normalized power variance. We use the actual channel vectors for each pilot symbol 𝐇𝐜∈ℂNf\mathbf{H_{c}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{f}} and the actual channel vectors for the pilot subcarriers 𝐇𝐩∈ℂNfLs\mathbf{H_{p}}\in\mathbb{C}^{\frac{N_{f}}{L_{s}}} to compute the correlation matrix by 𝐑𝐇𝐜​𝐇𝐩=𝔼⁡{𝐇𝐜​𝐇𝐩𝐇},𝐑𝐇𝐩​𝐇𝐩=𝔼⁡{𝐇𝐩​𝐇𝐩𝐇}\mathbf{R_{H_{c}H_{p}}}=\mathbb{E}\left\{\mathbf{H_{c}}\mathbf{H_{p}^{H}}\right\},\mathbf{R_{H_{p}H_{p}}}=\mathbb{E}\left\{\mathbf{H_{p}H_{p}^{H}}\right\}. These matrices are then substituted into (8) to calculate 𝐇^𝐌𝐌𝐒𝐄𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐨𝐭∈ℂNf\mathbf{\hat{H}_{MMSE}^{pilot}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{f}} for each pilot symbol. Bilinear interpolation is applied to this MMSE estimate to predict the complete channel matrix estimate. By incorporating ground-truth channel matrix of the environment channel and LS estimate as input, the MMSE method outperforms the LS estimate, but the implementation of the MMSE method is noncausal in practice.

Channel estimation neural networks take 𝐇^𝐥𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐨𝐭\mathbf{\hat{H}_{ls}^{pilot}} as input to infer 𝐇^∈ℂNf×Ns\mathbf{\hat{H}}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{f}\times N_{s}} as estimate for complete channel matrix. The real and imaginary parts of complex matrix are stored in the third dimension of both the real input and the real output. To demonstrate that the proposed method is effective across neural architectures, along with the Channelformer network, InterpolateNet in Luan and Thompson (2021) is also deployed as an example of low complexity estimator, with only 9,942 parameters.

3 Proposed design criteria for Doppler

The detailed operation of neural networks is difficult to understand as mathematical interpretability is still lacking. By using MSE loss for training, the neural network behavior is similar to MMSE filters as shown in Luan and Thompson (2025). As the rfr_{f} design has been discussed in Luan and Thompson (2025), this work only considers the rtr_{t} mismatch on a matched PDP. Except that Δ​ϵt=0\Delta\epsilon_{t}=0 under the matched Doppler spectrum of StD​(f)=StA​(f)S_{t}^{D}(f)=S_{t}^{A}(f), the Doppler spectrum of the designed channel is set to be the flat spectrum which has the theoretical formula of

S⁡(f)={12​fd,|f|≤fd,0,otherwise.S(f)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{2f_{d}},&|f|\leq f_{d},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (19)

It satisfies St​(f)=St​(−f)S_{t}(f)=S_{t}(-f) and when the boundary fdDf_{d}^{D} of the flat spectrum design exceeds fdAf_{d}^{A} of StA​(f)S_{t}^{A}(f), it has

∫−0.50.5𝐩⁡(i)​StA​(f)+σ2𝐩⁡(i)​StD​(f)+σ2​𝑑f=1,\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}\frac{\mathbf{p}(i)S_{t}^{A}(f)+\sigma^{2}}{\mathbf{p}(i)S_{t}^{D}(f)+\sigma^{2}}\,df=1, (20)

which gives Δ​ϵt\Delta\epsilon_{t} = 0. Therefore, by using the flat spectrum with a sufficiently large fdDf_{d}^{D} for design, the resulting filter should generalize well to any Doppler spectrum shape with a smaller fdf_{d} value. It should be noted that StD​(f)S_{t}^{D}(f) should be symmetric while the environment channel does not necessarily to be symmetric.

For the noncausal assumption, we do not need spectrum factorization for two-sided Mi​(f)M_{i}(f), and the noncausal corresponding coefficient is given by

𝐰i​(f)=𝐩⁡(i)​St​(f)𝐩⁡(i)​St​(f)+σ2.\mathbf{w}_{i}(f)=\frac{\mathbf{p}(i)S_{t}(f)}{\mathbf{p}(i)S_{t}(f)+\sigma^{2}}. (21)

Assume flat spectrum is deployed as the designed Doppler spectrum and the environment has a Doppler spectrum of StA​(f)S_{t}^{A}(f), the 𝐰iD​(f)\mathbf{w}_{i}^{D}(f) is given by

𝐰iD​(f)=𝐩⁡(i)​StD​(f)𝐩⁡(i)​StD​(f)+σ2={𝐩⁡(i)𝐩⁡(i)+2​σ2​fdD,|f|≤fdD,0,otherwise..\mathbf{w}_{i}^{D}(f)=\frac{\mathbf{p}(i)S_{t}^{D}(f)}{\mathbf{p}(i)S_{t}^{D}(f)+\sigma^{2}}=\begin{cases}\frac{\mathbf{p}(i)}{\mathbf{p}(i)+2\sigma^{2}f_{d}^{D}},&|f|\leq f_{d}^{D},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}. (22)

This result is independent of Doppler shifts, and |1−𝐰iD​(f)|2=(2​σ2𝐩⁡(i)​fd−1+2​σ2)2\left|1-\mathbf{w}_{i}^{D}(f)\right|^{2}=\left(\frac{2\sigma^{2}}{\mathbf{p}(i)f_{d}^{-1}+2\sigma^{2}}\right)^{2} is a constant across Doppler shifts. Therefore, each mismatch error under this flat spectrum design is provided by

Δ​ϵt,i\displaystyle\Delta\epsilon_{t,i} =𝐩⁡(i)​(2​σ2𝐩⁡(i)​fd−1+2​σ2)2​∫−0.50.5(StA​(f)−StD​(f))​𝑑f\displaystyle=\mathbf{p}(i)\left(\frac{2\sigma^{2}}{\mathbf{p}(i)f_{d}^{-1}+2\sigma^{2}}\right)^{2}\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}\left(S_{t}^{A}(f)-S_{t}^{D}(f)\right)\,df (23)
=𝐩⁡(i)​(2​σ2𝐩⁡(i)​fd−1+2​σ2)2​(∫−0.50.5StA​(f)​df−∫−0.50.5StD​(f)​df)\displaystyle=\mathbf{p}(i)\left(\frac{2\sigma^{2}}{\mathbf{p}(i)f_{d}^{-1}+2\sigma^{2}}\right)^{2}\left(\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}S_{t}^{A}(f)\,df-\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}S_{t}^{D}(f)\,df\right)
=0.\displaystyle=0.

For arbitrary normalized Doppler spectrum, it holds that ∫−0.50.5StA​(f)​𝑑f=∫−0.50.5StD​(f)​𝑑f=1\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}S_{t}^{A}(f)\,\mathrm{d}f=\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}S_{t}^{D}(f)\,\mathrm{d}f=1. Therefore, Δ​ϵt=0\Delta\epsilon_{t}=0 when the flat spectrum is deployed as StDS_{t}^{D} on any Doppler spectrum shape with a smaller value of fdf_{d}. Both causal and noncausal processing are commonly adopted in neural channel estimators (typically to predict for the whole slot), where pilot symbols embedded in intermediate OFDM symbols are used for time interpolation to predict the complete channel matrix of the whole slot. For example, the channel estimation at earlier symbols may depend on pilot symbols from later symbols, such as the first data OFDM symbol.

The benefit is, channel estimation neural networks will only require offline-training to perform well to unseen Doppler scenarios. We only need to consider the inference complexity because training is completely conducted offline. As regularization prevents overfitting as well as improving generalization slightly, the L2 regularization is set to 0 to remove the potential contribution. This is to show generalization is primarily due to the design criteria for training. Moreover, the proposed method is applicable to most neural networks because it imposes no specific constraints on their architectures.

4 Simulations

Normalized MSE (NMSE) is a performance metric that evaluates the normalized distance between the ground-truth channel matrix and its estimate for all resource elements in the slot, defined as

MSE⁡(𝐇^,𝐇)=𝔼⁡{‖𝐇^−𝐇‖F2}𝔼​{‖𝐇‖F2}.\mathrm{MSE}\left(\mathbf{\hat{H}},\mathbf{H}\right)=\frac{\mathbb{E}\left\{\left\Arrowvert\mathbf{\hat{H}}-\mathbf{H}\right\Arrowvert_{F}^{2}\right\}}{\mathbb{E}\left\{\left\Arrowvert\mathbf{H}\right\Arrowvert_{F}^{2}\right\}}. (24)

The offline-training dataset consists of 300,000 independent samples (95% for training and 5% for validation), which use the CE channel in Luan and Thompson (2025) as the default PDP. It ensures robust generalization to different PDPs, i.e. frequency-domain Interpolation. The mobile speed is set to 350km/h (maximum Doppler shift fdf_{d} of 1135Hz) with a fixed SNR of 20dB. This setting represents an intermediate high-mobility condition between the 300km/h and 500km/h HST test profiles specified in 3GPP TS 38.101-4 (3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), 2024). The deployed loss function is the MSE loss and the system configuration and training hyper-parameters are shown in Table. 1. It should be noted that this work only uses a very small subcarrier spacing fs​p​a​c​ef_{space} of 30kHz for high Doppler shifts scenarios. To average out Monte Carlo effects, each sample of the simulation curves is tested with 5,000 independent channel realizations.

4.1 Generalization to different Doppler spectrum and Doppler shifts

To show the generalization to different Doppler conditions, the offline-trained neural networks are tested with previously unseen Doppler spectra and Doppler shifts. We only use the flat Doppler spectrum and 1135Hz Doppler shifts for training neural networks, as provided by the proposed design criteria. This ensures that the trained neural networks generalize to the channels including but not just those channels, which are just examples to show the generalization results. Detailed expressions of the deployed Doppler spectra are shown in Appendix A.

Fig. 1a provides the MSE results for trained InterpolateNet tested on Doppler shifts from 0Hz to 350Hz when fdf_{d} has a Doppler spectrum of flat, Jakes, Bell, Guassian, Round, Asymmetric Jakes, Restricted Jakes or BiGuassian spectrum. For Doppler shifts from 0Hz to 1135Hz, both InterpolateNet and Channelformer achieve a flat NMSE performance for flat, Jakes, Bell, Round, Asymmetric Jakes, Restricted Jakes spectrum across the whole Doppler shift range. Compared to NMSE values at the Doppler shift of 0Hz, InterpolateNet increase NMSE values by 0.0226 on Guassian spectrum and 0.0088 on BiGuassian spectrum at the Doppler shift of 1135Hz, while Channelformer increase NMSE values by 0.0226 on Guassian spectrum and 0.0088 on BiGuassian spectrum. The LS estimate and the MMSE method have NMSE values from 0.39 to 0.40 and from 0.0002 to 0.0262, respectively. Because the MMSE method cooperates with bilinear interpolation for time-domain interpolation, it results in worse time-domain interpolation performance. Therefore, neural network methods can outperform the MMSE methods in a high Doppler shift range.

Except for BiGuassian and Guassian spectrum, both InterpolateNet and Channelformer achieve almost identical MSE performance across these unseen Doppler spectra and Doppler shifts from 0Hz to 1135Hz, only with a slight variation of 0.00072 for InterpolateNet and 0.00065 for Channelformer at Doppler shift of 1135Hz. For Guassian and BiGuassian spectrum, InterpolateNet achieves a NMSE value of 0.0284 and 0.0146 at Doppler shift of 1135Hz, respectively. Channelformer has a NMSE value of 0.0271 and 0.0122 for each, which also show a slight variation shown in Fig. 1.

4.2 Validation of preservation of generalization to PDPs

After demonstrating the generalization to Doppler shifts and Doppler spectrum, we evaluate if this proposed design criteria will damage the design criteria for generalization to PDPs proposed in Luan and Thompson (2025), while time correlation and frequency correlation are separable.

Fig. 2a provides the generalization property of offline-trained neural networks to different PDPs. For each path, the corresponding Doppler shifts have a randomly assigned Doppler spectrum. From the simulation results on these example channels, both InterpolateNet and Channelformer achieve almost identical NMSE values across these unseen PDPs. Fig. 2b and Fig. 2c show the NMSE values when trained InterpolateNet and Channelformer are tested on randomly generated channels and each NMSE point is averaged by 50 slots. Each channel realization has a path number MM randomly selected from 1 to 15, and the path delays are confined within a maximum delay spread of the duration of CP to emulate practical propagation characteristics. Up to three early paths are uniformly distributed within the first 700ns, subject to a minimum inter-path spacing constraint to prevent unrealistic clustering. The remaining paths are uniformly distributed over the interval from 700ns to the duration of CP, resulting in a sparser late-arrival structure. Each ama_{m} follows an exponential distribution to capture the typical power decay behavior of multipath channels. After power normalization, the strongest path is enforced within the early components. For offline-trained InterpolateNet and Channelformer, the mean value is 0.0046 and 0.0042 respectively; the upper boundary of the best-performing 10% and the lower boundary of the worst-performing 10% are 0.0037 and 0.0052 for InterpolateNet, 0.0030 and 0.0052 for Channelformer. These results demonstrate that the proposed design criteria do not compromise generalization to channels with unseen PDPs.

4.3 Ablation experiments: Validation of the proposed design criteria

As shown in Section. 4.1, trained neural networks exhibit strong generalization to Doppler by following the proposed design criteria. Simultaneously, we intentionally violate this design criteria for training to observe NMSE degradation, and this ablation experiment is used to understand the contribution of our proposal.

Fig. 3a and Fig. 3b provide the NMSE values for InterpolateNets and Channelformers trained with different single fdDf_{d}^{D} and tested on Doppler shifts from 0Hz to 1135Hz with StD​(f)=StA​(f)S_{t}^{D}(f)=S_{t}^{A}(f) (flat spectrum). These curves increase as the Doppler shift increases. Neural networks trained with Doppler shift of 1135Hz achieve almost identical NMSE across these Doppler shifts. For example, InterpolateNet and Channelformer only have a slight variation from 0.0058 to 0.0068 and from 0.0045 to 0.0054 respectively. However, when the unseen fdAf_{d}^{A} are larger than the fdDf_{d}^{D} used for training, trained neural networks exhibit increased NMSE on these unseen fdAf_{d}^{A}. For example, for Channelformer trained with fdf_{d} = 681Hz, it has NMSE values of 0.0038, 0.0057 and 0.0108 at the maximum Doppler shifts of 681Hz, 908Hz and 1135Hz. Especially, for neural networks trained with lower Doppler shifts, they perform better on low Doppler shifts and degrade significantly on high Doppler range. For example, InterpolateNet trained with fdf_{d} of 0Hz achieves the best NMSE among these trained InterpolateNets but exhibits the most severe increase on other unseen Doppler shifts. It has a NMSE of 0.0016 at 0Hz while the corresponding NMSE value of 0.3203 at 1135Hz, which indicates random prediction at high Doppler shifts. The increase in NMSE is mainly down to fdD<fdAf_{d}^{D}<f_{d}^{A}, while the NMSE values are stable when fdA≤fdDf_{d}^{A}\leq f_{d}^{D}.

Fig. 3c and Fig. 3d provide the NMSE values for InterpolateNets and Channelformers trained with different Doppler spectrum with fdDf_{d}^{D} = 640Hz, and then tested on these spectra with fdAf_{d}^{A} = 640Hz. InterpolateNet and Channelformer trained with flat spectrum has only slight NMSE variation of 0.00067 and 0.000628 among these spectra, which is the smallest variation compared to neural networks trained with other candidate spectrum. It should be noted that only the variation caused by channel mismatch is evaluated to show the generalization property. The aim is to ensure robustness against Doppler mismatch rather than to achieve the minimum estimate error among these spectra. From these simulation results, neural networks trained with flat spectrum and fdA≤fdDf_{d}^{A}\leq f_{d}^{D} achieve good generalization to unseen Doppler spectra and Doppler shifts, while violating the proposed design criteria leads to an increase in NMSE.

5 Conclusion

We propose design criteria to generate the training data for channel estimation neural networks that achieve strong generalization to unseen Doppler shifts and Doppler spectra. It ensures trained neural networks perform time-domain interpolation well across new and previously unseen channels, which retain the superior performance for practical implementation of channel estimation neural networks. Moreover, the proposed design criteria is applicable for most neural networks because no specific neural architecture is required. From the simulation results, trained neural networks achieve robust performance across different Doppler shifts and Doppler spectra. Moreover, the proposed design criteria do not damage the generalization to channels with unseen power delay profiles as shown in the simulation results.

Δ​ϵt=1Nf​∑i=1Nf𝐩⁡(i)​∫−0.50.5(StA​(f)−StD​(f))​|1−𝐰iD​(f)|2​𝑑f.\Delta\epsilon_{t}=\frac{1}{N_{f}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{f}}\mathbf{p}(i)\int_{-0.5}^{0.5}\left(S_{t}^{A}(f)-S_{t}^{D}(f)\right)\left|1-\mathbf{w}_{i}^{D}(f)\right|^{2}\mathrm{d}f. (35)

The deployed Doppler spectra are described as follows. The Rounded Doppler spectrum has the theoretical formula of

S⁡(f)=11.168​fd​[1−1.72​(ffd)2+0.785​(ffd)4],|f|≤fd.S(f)=\frac{1}{1.168f_{d}}\left[1-1.72\left(\frac{f}{f_{d}}\right)^{2}+0.785\left(\frac{f}{f_{d}}\right)^{4}\right],\quad|f|\leq f_{d}. (36)

The Bell Doppler spectrum has the theoretical formula of

S⁡(f)=3π​fd1+9​(ffd)2,|f|≤fd,S(f)=\frac{\frac{3}{\pi f_{d}}}{1+9\left(\frac{f}{f_{d}}\right)^{2}},\quad|f|\leq f_{d}, (37)

The Asymmetric Jakes Doppler spectrum has the theoretical formula of

S⁡(f)\displaystyle S(f) =Aaπ​fd​1−(f/fd)2,−fd≤fmin≤f≤fmax≤fd,\displaystyle=\frac{A_{a}}{\pi f_{d}\sqrt{1-\left(f/f_{d}\right)^{2}}},\quad-f_{d}\leq f_{\min}\leq f\leq f_{\max}\leq f_{d}, (38)
whereAa\displaystyle\text{where}\quad A_{a} =11π​[sin−1⁡(fmaxfd)−sin−1⁡(fminfd)]andfmin=0,fmax=fd.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\dfrac{1}{\pi}\left[\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{f_{\max}}{f_{d}}\right)-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{f_{\min}}{f_{d}}\right)\right]}\ \mathrm{and}\ f_{\min}=0,f_{\max}=f_{d}.

The Restricted Jakes Doppler spectrum has the theoretical formula of

S⁡(f)\displaystyle S(f) =Arπ​fd​1−(f/fd)2,0≤fmin≤|f|≤fmax≤fd,\displaystyle=\frac{A_{r}}{\pi f_{d}\sqrt{1-\left(f/f_{d}\right)^{2}}},\quad 0\leq f_{\min}\leq|f|\leq f_{\max}\leq f_{d}, (39)
whereAr\displaystyle\text{where}\quad A_{r} =12π​[sin−1⁡(fmaxfd)−sin−1⁡(fminfd)]andfmin=0.2fd,fmax=0.8fd.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\frac{2}{\pi}\left[\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{f_{\max}}{f_{d}}\right)-\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{f_{\min}}{f_{d}}\right)\right]}\ \mathrm{and}\ f_{\min}=0.2f_{d},f_{\max}=0.8f_{d}.

The Gaussian Doppler spectrum has the theoretical formula of

SG​(f)=12​π​σ2​e−f22​σ2,S_{G}(f)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}e^{-\frac{f^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}}, (40)

where σ=12​fd\sigma=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}f_{d}.
